sections.title: Studies in History/Theory: Water School/Landscape History Cooperative (A)
sections.description: What if rivers, waterways, channels—often used as “sewers” (from the English term seaward) in North America during the 19th and 20th centuries—instead offer vital sites of historical memory and watery futures? In Spring 2027, the Water School graduate seminar partners with Bartram’s Garden—a home for horticulture, the first nationally landmarked landscape, and North America's oldest surviving botanic garden. Through close collaboration with Bartram’s staff and Penn partners in CHOP and Environmental Studies, alongside engagement with archival materials housed at Penn, the Fairmount Park Collection, and throughout Philadelphia, students will explore topics including hydrological legacies, water quality pasts, bog plant humanities, industrial development and land grab dynamics along the Schuylkill, and environmental justice concepts and histories focused on water ecologies—both locally and in relation to transatlantic/transhemispheric contexts. Emphasizing a method-to-action approach, the course centers on community-led and co-created public histories that speak to contemporary practices of river restoration and watershed justice in landscape studies. This semester’s course focuses on Bartram’s Garden's North Mile (and the water's edge and proposed Field Station) and is the second ABCS course (Academically Based Community Service) in a five-year-long commitment with the organization. The final project will be co-created with the Bartram's team.
